title: The breath and the Name
hookLine: the yogis speak of breath practice; Nanak points to the Name within the breath

cards: A breath went in just now. Nobody asked it to. Another will come, and another, all day, through meetings and traffic and sleep, without a single instruction from you.

The yogis who sit across from Guru Nanak in the Sidh Gosht had made a whole discipline of that quiet traffic: how to hold the breath, slow it, steer it, master it. They bring it up, and Nanak doesn't wave it away.
He answers. But he points somewhere they might not expect.

teach.b: Start with what the yogis brought to the mountain. In the dialogue, theirs is a path of discipline: postures, earrings, the patched coat, and work with the breath. The breath was something to train.
Nanak's answers, all through the Sidh Gosht, keep coming back to the Word, the Shabad, held inside. So when talk turns to the breath, the poem doesn't tell anyone to stop.
Read beside the rest of his answers, the question shifts: not how long the breath is held, but what it carries. That idea runs all through the Guru Granth Sahib.
Guru Arjan, in the Sukhmani, puts it in a phrase Sikhs still use: saas saas simrahu Gobind.
In paraphrase: remember the Lord with every breath, and the worry inside the mind lifts. Notice the shape of that. Not one great breath held for a long time.
Every breath, the ordinary ones: the one at the red light, the one in your sleep.
The word for this remembering is simran, and some Sikhs do it by letting the Name, Waheguru, ride the breath in and out, quietly, without forcing anything. So here's the turn.

For the yogis, the breath was a thing to conquer. In this reading, it becomes a carrier, and what it carries matters more than how long you can hold it. Nothing here asks anyone to give up a breathing exercise.
The Guru's point, as tradition reads it, is that the breath was never the goal. The Name inside it was.

how: Sikhs practice simran by repeating the Name, often Waheguru, and some match it to the breath, silently or aloud; the Sukhmani, with its call to remember with every breath, is recited in homes and gurdwaras.

games.q: what does “the breath and the name” mean?
o: holding one long breath to master the body
remembering the Name with every ordinary breath
a breathing drill to calm the body before prayer

games.q: what's inside the breath and the Name — tap the pairs.
p: points to what the breath carries

s: in the Sidh Gosht, Nanak mocks the yogis' breath practice
he answers them and moves the center: the Word steadies a person, not the technique.
Guru Arjan's phrase is about every breath, not one long held breath
saas saas: remember with every breath, ordinary ones included.
simran means forcing the breath into a pattern
simran is remembering; some Sikhs let the Name ride the breath without forcing it.

games.q: the yogis raise their discipline of the breath. you're Nanak. what do you say?
o: that what matters is the Name the breath carries.
that he can hold his breath longer than they can.
games.why: he answers without mocking, and turns the question: the Word inside steadies a person, not mastery of the breath.

practice: Don't change your breathing at all; just let ten breaths come.
If you'd like, let Waheguru ride each one, wahe on the way in, guru on the way out, or use a word that matters to you, or simply count, and if you lose count, start again without scolding yourself.
When the ten are done, keep sitting, and notice that the breath keeps going without you.

wordCard.voice: The breath and the Name. In the Sidh Gosht, the yogis train the breath; Nanak points to what it carries. Guru Arjan's phrase: remember with every breath. Today's word.

orig.note: remembrance: keeping the Name in mind, often by repeating it.

carryVoice: Your line: the name in the breath. Every ordinary breath can carry it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sukhmani, Gauri Mahala 5 ('saas saas simrahu Gobind')
